clue.text: "Destructive arms limitation? No ta, leave it out!" — Blair's and Bush's thing?

indicators.note: something destructive wrecks its target, so the letters of the two words are smashed and rebuilt
telling the solver to leave out the words just named, no and ta, drops those four letters from the phrase before the jumble

parts.note: taken as written: the phrase that is cut down and jumbled
taken as written
the word no; its two letters come out of the phrase, where they stand the other way round

explanation.surface: A sarcastic slogan against arms control, as if Blair and Bush were refusing to give up weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: The removed letters need not sit together: take N, O, T and A out of the fourteen letters and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye cast the two leaders of the Iraq War as warmongers, so a belief in armed force is their shared obsession.

clue.text: Daily brain diet loses kid

indicators.note: losing a brat, a kid, strips those four letters from the outside of the phrase, leaving the run inside

parts.note: taken as written: the answer lies inside these words

explanation.surface: A newspaper's brainy healthy-eating plan drops its children's section.
explanation.walkthrough: The kid is a brat: three of its letters come off the front and one off the back. The Indie is the nickname of The Independent, a British daily paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily is a newspaper published every weekday, and this one is a nickname for The Independent.

clue.text: Stiff but lacking the will

definitions.meaning: slang for a corpse, not rigid or formal
not missing determination but having made no legal will

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone rigid but listless; the word means dying without having made a will, which a corpse may well have done.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dies without a valid testament is said to die this way, and the estate passes by law.

clue.text: Stupid sailor's crap going topless

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, with the possessive S

indicators.note: a word going topless loses its first letter

parts.note: a turd is a lump of excrement

explanation.surface: A sailor's idiotic rubbish, delivered half-naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests a bare-breasted sailor; here it means the word loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Absurd means ridiculous or wildly unreasonable, which is foolish.

clue.text: A leader rejected, in short, is without depth

definitions.meaning: a party leader thrown out by his colleagues: the Tory leader ousted in October 2003
his initials are made of 'is' round D for depth, and a shallow lightweight is without depth

explanation.walkthrough: The Conservative leader ousted in 2003 was known by his initials IDS: IS outside D for depth. The clue also mocks him as shallow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Conservative Party leader removed by a vote of no confidence among his own MPs in October 2003.

clue.text: Unstable! Bush: "Damn! Time to replace new sloppy medical treatments"

indicators.note: unstable things fall apart and settle in a new order
time to replace new means the letter for time takes the place of the letter for new

parts.note: taken as written: the President's name
taken as written: his oath

explanation.surface: George Bush cursing about unstable and messy healthcare reforms.
explanation.walkthrough: The words are swapped before the jumble: N in the two names becomes T.
explanation.definitionFit: Spa therapies where the patient is immersed in warm mud are literally sloppy cures.

clue.text: Given new top, clasps tits

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is swapped for a different one

parts.note: to clasp someone is to hug them

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of someone being groped after a change of bra.
explanation.walkthrough: The replacement letter comes from nowhere in the clue; only the crossings and the definition fix it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are vulgar British slang words for a woman's breasts.

clue.text: Patriarch, firm, wants poke outside

indicators.note: the poke goes outside, wrapping round the company

parts.note: a jab is a quick poke

explanation.surface: A company boss who wants a dig taken at someone outside.
explanation.walkthrough: CO, company, is the usual crossword firm.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament forefather of the twelve tribes of Israel, son of Isaac.

clue.text: Goolies twisted and crushed by great rock enthusiast

indicators.note: being crushed by something means being squeezed inside it

parts.note: GT is a standard abbreviation of great

indicators.note: twisted letters are wrung into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: British slang for testicles

explanation.surface: A rock fan's testicles mangled and crushed in a mosh pit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock enthusiast' suggests music; here it is stone. Goolies is British slang for testicles.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientist who studies rocks and the structure of the earth is literally keen on stones.

clue.text: Do a Piers Morgan — perverted bore

indicators.note: perverted literally means turned the wrong way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a bore is a tidal wave surging up a river, so a tide

explanation.surface: A jibe that Piers Morgan is a twisted bore.
explanation.walkthrough: Piers Morgan was then editor of the Daily Mirror. 'Bore' looks like an insult but means the tidal surge up a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing what Piers Morgan did for a living means running a newspaper, the job of its editor.

clue.text: Twist and cut off balls of Blair aide?

parts.note: to twist the facts is to put a spin on them
to doctor an animal is to castrate it

explanation.surface: A violent fantasy of mangling and castrating one of Tony Blair's advisers.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair's press team, led by Alastair Campbell, were notorious for manipulating the news.
explanation.definitionFit: A political press officer who puts the best slant on stories was a key figure in Blair's Downing Street.

clue.text: Condemned Saracen sure did ditch Fergie (not hard) and primitive urges

indicators.note: to ditch things is to get rid of them, so these letters are dropped from the phrase

parts.note: taken as written; that the answer then lies inside these words is no coincidence but the setter's design, the duchess and the id being cut from either end

indicators.note: not here means the letter for hard is left off the name

parts.note: Fergie is Sarah Ferguson, the Duchess of York
in Freud the id is the seat of primitive instincts

explanation.surface: A Saracen, doomed, ditches the Duchess of York and his base instincts.
explanation.walkthrough: One name comes off the front of the phrase and the Freudian id off the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To be censured is to be formally criticised or blamed, much as the condemned are.

clue.text: Shifty Blair not right, no, for Britain

indicators.note: a shifty arrangement is one that moves around, so the letters are rearranged
not tells the solver to leave out the letter for right

parts.note: taken as written: the Prime Minister's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: Tony Blair is shifty and no good for the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifty' reads as a jibe at Blair; it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Albion is an old poetic name for Britain, from the white cliffs of Dover.

clue.text: Having dipped end of todger in butter, it's no long tender

indicators.note: dipping one thing into another puts it inside
in confirms where the dipped letter ends up

parts.note: a butter is an animal that butts, such as a goat

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: a todger is British slang for a penis; its end is the final letter

explanation.surface: A smutty kitchen mishap: a penis dipped in butter is no longer firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' is the animal that butts, not the dairy spread. A todger is British slang for a penis.
explanation.definitionFit: This old English silver coin is long withdrawn, so it is no longer legal tender.

clue.text: Cheated and removed bodice, literally?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: taken off by tearing, as in a bodice-ripper romance

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal reading of the slang phrase: a bodice torn away.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang for being swindled also describes clothing torn violently from someone.

clue.text: Hint: he's broken with it, being surrounded by crap

indicators.note: broken pieces are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tip-off that someone has gone bankrupt and is deep in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hint' looks like the definition; it is part of the jumble, and the definition sits at the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: The vulgar idiom for being in serious trouble pictures someone literally mired in excrement.

clue.text: Penultimate selection of names of colleagues Clare's got it in for?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the final candidates chosen before the winner

definitions.text: colleagues Clare's got it in for?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Clare Short's roll of grudges, a list belonging to Short

explanation.walkthrough: Clare Short resigned from Blair's cabinet in 2003 and attacked her former colleagues; her list of enemies would be hers, a Short list.
explanation.definitionFit: A reduced field of candidates from which the final choice is made is the next-to-last stage of selection.

clue.text: Broadcasting the tales of Linford Christie and his sort?

indicators.note: broadcasting in the old farming sense means scattering seed, so the letters are scattered

parts.note: taken as written: the gossip being spread

explanation.surface: Tabloid gossip being spread about the Olympic sprinter Linford Christie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcasting' suggests radio or television; it means scattering. Linford Christie was a British Olympic 100m champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Christie was a sprinter, and those like him are track and field competitors.

clue.text: It checks those who go beyond the limit, getting pissed, wearing thong

definitions.text: It checks those who go beyond the limit

indicators.note: a thing wearing a garment sits inside it

parts.note: a thong is a strap of leather
the literal sense, urinated, rather than British slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A drunk driver in a thong being stopped by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' and 'limit' suggest drink-driving, where pissed is British slang for drunk; here it means urinated.
explanation.definitionFit: A police device or stretch of road set up to catch motorists breaking the speed limit.

clue.text: Attractive female who's willing to have child with Conservative — no alternative

parts.note: a tot is a small child

indicators.note: no alternative means the word for an alternative is removed

parts.note: or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A Tory MP's fling with a pretty woman who wants his baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Totty' is British slang, faintly sexist, for attractive young women.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a sexually attractive woman, usually used collectively by leering men.

clue.text: Given a wee application, it's said, as an engine part

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so the answer matches the phrase by ear

parts.note: urinated on, a crude way of putting 'pissed on'

explanation.surface: A dog relieving itself on a car part.
explanation.walkthrough: A wee is British informal for urination.
explanation.definitionFit: A piston is the sliding cylinder driven by combustion inside a car motor.

clue.text: Livingstone will, reportedly (somewhere for the mutt during the hols?)

definitions.text: somewhere for the mutt during the hols?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the answer matches the phrase in pronunciation

parts.note: Ken Livingstone, then Mayor of London, shortened with the contraction for will

explanation.surface: Ken Livingstone, Mayor of London, deciding where to leave the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Livingstone was Mayor of London; his first name plus 'll for will gives the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A boarding kennel looks after dogs while their owners are away on holiday.

clue.text: Pleased to get new leader (number two's dumped here)

indicators.note: getting a new leader means the first letter is swapped

parts.note: happy means pleased

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the word new, whose first letter becomes the new leader

explanation.surface: A party happy with its new leader while the deputy is thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number two' reads as a deputy leader; here it is childish slang for excrement.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby's absorbent pad, known in the US as a diaper, is where a toddler's poo ends up.

clue.text: US agents in street, one turned over Bill — "pain in the rear"

indicators.note: the agents sit in the middle of the street abbreviation

parts.note: the CIA is the American intelligence agency

indicators.note: turning a word over sets its letters backwards

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: An American spy on the street complaining about a troublesome man named Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pain in the rear' sounds like a nuisance, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sciatica is nerve pain running from the lower back through the buttock and down the leg.

clue.text: Bound to give head to Brenda

parts.note: to cap something is to put a top on it
Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose royal cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A crude suggestion about the Queen and oral sex.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called the Queen Brenda; ER is Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: To caper is to leap or skip about playfully, as a bound is a jump.

clue.text: One American to another: "Take out half of commie with missile"

indicators.note: removing half of a six-letter word leaves its first three letters

parts.note: taken as written: slang for a communist
the Patriot is an American surface-to-air missile

explanation.surface: One American urging another to kill a communist with a rocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take out' looks like the definition, meaning kill; it tells the solver to drop half the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Each American is a fellow countryman of the next, someone from the same nation.

clue.text: Cyclops gets to make out — it's child play!

parts.note: the setter's pseudonym, so the setter speaking of themself
to make something out is to spy or spot it

explanation.surface: The setter boasting about a sexual encounter, then claiming it is just kids' stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' suggests snogging; here it means to catch sight of.
explanation.definitionFit: A guessing game for children where one player names something they can see by its first letter.

clue.text: Doubtful erection saint got rid of

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes those letters

parts.note: a stiffy is British slang for an erection

explanation.surface: A lewd scene: a saint gets rid of an erection whose existence is in doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubtful erection' reads as one phrase; the definition is the first word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Iffy is informal for uncertain, dubious or of questionable quality.

clue.text: Crap controllers rubbished script she devised about North

indicators.note: about puts the jumble round the compass letter
rubbished words are trashed and thrown together again

parts.note: taken as written: the words being rubbished

explanation.surface: Censors savaging a script written by a woman from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crap controllers' reads as useless bosses; here crap is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sphincters are ring muscles, including the anal one that holds back excrement.
